selected_topic.title: Vincent Coleman’s telegraph warning during the 1917 Halifax Explosion
selected_topic.angle: A telegraph operator’s last warning is often simplified into a certain train rescue. The source record is disputed, but the message’s wider, documented effect was to alert railway stations and help trigger relief trains.
selected_topic.viewer_value: Viewers learn how one message could matter even when the famous rescue claim is uncertain: it warned a regional rail network and connected a devastated city to incoming aid.

audience: General English-language history Shorts viewers who respond to a compact, human-scale story with a factual reversal and a concrete consequence. This is an editorial hypothesis, not measured audience data.

selection.strongest_alternative: The James Caird crossing: dramatic and well documented, but its central survival arc is already a famous canonical adventure; Coleman’s story offers a more surprising correction between legend and record.
selection.objection_to_selected: Coleman’s role in stopping Train No. 10 is contested, so a standard hero-rescue hook risks overstating certainty. The selected framing discloses the disagreement and pays off through the documented network warning and relief response.

promise_payoff.promise: A last telegraph message sent just before a catastrophic explosion; what did it actually accomplish?
promise_payoff.verified_object: Vincent Coleman’s telegraph message, recorded in the Maritime Museum of the Atlantic account; exact wording varies across contemporary reports, so narration paraphrases it.
promise_payoff.opening_confirmation: Open on Halifax’s 9:05 explosion, then establish a message sent minutes earlier.
promise_payoff.payoff: The message alerted railway stations beyond Halifax and helped set six relief trains moving; whether it stopped Train No. 10 remains unresolved.
promise_payoff.visual_motif: Telegraph key/message line leading from station to rail map; later resolve into inbound relief trains.

uncertainty: Whether Coleman personally stopped Train No. 10 is unclear in the Maritime Museum’s review of conflicting accounts. Do not say he certainly saved its approximately 300 passengers.
Contemporary wording of the telegram varied; script paraphrases rather than presents a supposedly exact transcript.

sources.claim: Coleman sent a warning; the station was about 750 feet from the blast; the account says the message would be heard from Halifax to Truro, reports six relief trains, and explicitly states the Train No. 10 evidence is unclear and conflicting.
sources.location: Sections opening lines 25-33; Explosion lines 42-47; Results lines 54-67.

sources.claim: SS Mont-Blanc and SS Imo collided on Dec. 6, 1917; Mont-Blanc carried explosives, burned for about 20 minutes, and exploded at 9:05; roughly 2,000 died.
Communications were disrupted; six relief trains arrived the day of the blast.

A 1918 disaster-office narrative records that Coleman telephoned a warning about a burning munitions ship; this contemporary personal narrative supports that he warned of the danger, but not a definitive account of the passenger train outcome.

Source check for strongest alternative: Shackleton’s party salvaged three lifeboats; the James Caird crew reached South Georgia but could not reach the whaling stations by boat from their landing point.
